inline.s: Moonlight is the Chinese [name]; Jivaka is Sanskrit, here rendered "firmly living." At birth, in one hand he held a medicine bag and in the other a needle-case. Formerly he had vowed to be a physician, curing the sick and keeping them alive, so he was named for his virtue. He was the son of the Amra woman. Both were exceedingly wise, plainly showing them to be virtuous ministers.

The Veda scriptures are the worldly classics; sometimes written Veda, the Sanskrit differs slightly. Like the histories of this land, they record the affairs of that country. To covet the throne and kill one's father is already a great evil; to slay one's mother without the Way has never been heard of through the ages. In western India there are four castes, which gather within themselves all castes: the Ksatriya and the Brahmana are the two honored ones; the Vaisya and the Sudra are the two lowly ones. The Ksatriya is the royal caste. The Candala is here called the slayer, the sort of executioner found in this land. Since the king was without the Way, a worthy minister would not aid him, and so he could not bear to remain. Pressing his sword and stepping back, he displayed his authority so as to make him afraid. (Lingzhi's Commentary)

At that time Ajatasatru was seized with terror and panic, and said to Jivaka, "Will you not act for me?" Jivaka replied, "Great king, be sure not to harm your mother!" When the king heard these words, he repented and begged for deliverance. Straightway he put down his sword and refrained from harming his mother.

King Ajatasatru was alarmed and fearful; when a worthy minister leaves the land, the altars of state must be endangered. "Will you not act for me" are words begging for deliverance. "Act" means "to assist." (Lingzhi's Commentary)
Wu 3: The decree to confine her in seclusion.
By edict he spoke to the inner officers, confining her in the deep palace, not allowing her to come out again.
Jivaka remonstrated again and again, and the king repented and followed him. That he decreed her confinement in the deep palace is the origin of her awakening. (Lingzhi's Commentary)

The king's intent: if the mother were not confined, the father could never die; if he wished the father to die, he must confine the mother. So he decreed to the inner officers to shut her up in the deep palace. (Elaboration)
Ding 2: The compassionate mother's plea for help, in three parts.
First, because of the confinement she begs the Buddha.
Second, the Buddha knows and goes. Third, in grief she asks for the Dharma.
Wu 1: Because of the confinement she begs the Buddha.

At that time Vaidehi, having been confined, was grieved and haggard; from afar she turned toward Vulture Peak, paid homage to the Buddha, and spoke these words: "O World-Honored One, in former times you always sent Ananda to comfort and question me. Now I am grieved, and the World-Honored One's dignity is too great for me to see. I beg you to send Maudgalyayana and the venerable Ananda to meet with me." Having spoken these words, she wept tears like rain, and from afar bowed to the Buddha.

The commentary says: Why did Vaidehi ask to see Maudgalyayana and Ananda? Maudgalyayana was her teacher of the gate, Ananda the Buddha's attendant. They had formerly always taught her, so she specially sought to see them. Dwelling in the deep palace, she dared not ask in particular; inwardly detesting this defiled world, she longed to be born in the Pure Land. She wished the two of them to convey her intent and beg the Buddha. I privately reflect: the lady was confined; first, she could not save the king from death, and second, she had no way to face the golden face [of the Buddha]; there was nothing to be done. She could only bow from afar and pray, hence the words "and spoke these words." Formerly, whenever the palace had affairs, the Buddha always sent his attendant to inquire; now, in her distress and grief, the Buddha's mind-reading would surely perceive it; not daring to beg the Buddha to come in person, she wished the two to meet her. Maudgalyayana is called "teacher of the gate": he was Bimbisara's teacher. It was said earlier: "Great Maudgalyayana is my friend and kinsman; I beg you to show compassion and give me the eight precepts," so he is the teacher of the eight precepts. And that she also asked for Ananda was to have them convey her request and beg the Buddha personally to bestow the Dharma's grace. "Having spoken these words" and the following three clauses ask for the Dharma. The commentary says: weeping tears like rain, hoping for the Buddha's compassion; bowing from afar to the Buddha. Earlier she had already bowed, and now she bows again, showing her earnestness. (Elaboration)
Wu 2: The Buddha knows and goes.

Before she had even raised her head, at that time the World-Honored One, on Vulture Peak, knew what Vaidehi had in mind, and straightway commanded Great Maudgalyayana and Ananda to come through the sky; the Buddha vanished from Vulture Peak and appeared in the royal palace.
Knowing what was in her mind is the intellect of knowing others' minds. Riding the sky in vanishing and appearing is the transcendent power of spiritual freedom. (Lingzhi's Commentary)

At that time Vaidehi, having bowed, raised her head and saw the World-Honored One Sakyamuni Buddha, his body purple-gold in color, seated on a lotus of a hundred jewels, Maudgalyayana attending on the left and Ananda on the right; Sakra, Brahma, the world-protectors and the various devas, in the empty sky, rained heavenly flowers everywhere and held them as offerings.

In seeing the Buddha there were four particular excellences: first, the color of his body; second, the lotus seat; third, the attendants left and right; and fourth, the offerings of the devas. Sakra is Indra; in full, Sakyamunindra... rather, Sakyamunindra means "lord of the thirty-three heavens," i.e., the lord of the Trayastrimsa heavens. Brahma is the Great Brahma king, lord of the form realm. The world-protectors are the four great kings and so on. An ancient commentary asks: Bimbisara and Vaidehi both asked for disciples; why did he first send disciples and afterwards go in person? What is the meaning? There are two explanations: first, Ajatasatru had killed his father; if the Buddha went in person, it would arouse resentment and enmity, and this was to protect his mind. Second, to carry on the Buddha-Dharma, one must entrust it to the king; since Bimbisara was certain to die and Ajatasatru to ascend the throne, if the Buddha went in person it would be obstructed and could not proceed, and this was to protect the Dharma. Vaidehi had none of these [obstructions], so going in person was no impediment. (Lingzhi's Commentary)

The Direct Pointing commentary says: "Question: The king and the queen both requested the disciples; why did the king send a messenger while the queen went herself? Answer: There are three intentions. First, Bimbisara wished to receive the precepts and hear the Dharma, so a person could be sent to transmit them; Vaidehi wished to seek rebirth in the Pure Land, which the Buddha could not open without coming himself. Second, if he went in person to the king, Ajatasatru would think that his father was plotting with him for power, and his enmity would be heavy, leading to the extinction of Dharma and Sangha, an unforgivable offense; but going in person to the queen, Ajatasatru would think the mother had no plan for rule, so his resentment would be lighter; though he confined both parents, the offense could still be repented. Third, the king is a man, so a disciple could be sent to instruct him without further resentment; the queen is a woman, and so the teacher and student must come together to overcome the doubts and slanders."
Wu 3: In grief she asks for the Dharma, in two parts.
First, asking about the cause of former lives.
Second, asking about the place of rebirth.
Ji 1: Asking about the cause of former lives.

At that time Vaidehi, seeing the World-Honored One, tore off her own necklaces, threw her whole body to the ground, and weeping loudly said to the Buddha, "O World-Honored One! For what offense in a former life have I borne this evil son? And what karmic causes did the World-Honored One have, to be related to Devadatta as kinsmen?

The cause of the former life has two meanings: first, she asks what offense in her former life gave birth to this evil, rebellious son; second, what karmic relation the World-Honored One had to be regarded as kin to Devadatta. (Elaboration)

The passage has two sections: first, making obeisance to express reverence. Imprisoned so long, she did not expect to meet the Buddha; grief and joy filled her breast, with no time for delay, so she broke the necklaces from her neck and held them to offer the Buddha. She threw her body to the ground to exhaust her sincerity. (Lingzhi's Commentary)

Next, the direct question about the former cause. Between me and my son, love issues from nature; between the Buddha and his brother-in-law, affection is like the natural bonds of kinship. Yet they turned to harming one another, so there must be a past cause. She mainly reproaches herself, and at the same time asks the Tathagata. But this is merely grieving over past karma as the ground for making her plea. The sutras and vinaya say much, that the Buddha and Devadatta, from cause to fruit, were always troubling one another. This is presumably the great expedient shadow-play, and not a real matter. That is, the Lotus Sutra says: "Because of the good friend Devadatta, I was made complete in the six paramitas," down to "in future, after immeasurable aeons, he shall attain Buddhahood, named Tathagata King of Heaven," and so on. (Lingzhi's Commentary)

Under "said," she asks to be shown the two causes. "What offense" is the past cause; "this evil son" is the present fruit, asking about the cause of her own family and kin. The relation is as explained before. Under "World-Honored," she asks about the Tathagata's relation to his kin: in former times, at the time of Dipamkara Buddha, Yajnadata wished to give his daughter in marriage, and there was an aged Brahman ascetic, Sumati, who sought to be the son-in-law, wise and with a handsome face; at that time Sakyamuni, as the young man Manava Muni... rather, as the young brahmin youth, of fine appearance, having studied with the sage of jewels and become accomplished, came from afar and met Sumati in debate; Sumati was refuted, Yajnadata rejoiced and gave his daughter in marriage, and Sumati, in furious rage, vowed that in the future, life after life, he would continually trouble [the Buddha]. Sumati was Devadatta; the daughter was Gopi, as in the Birth Sutra.

...One should know that Ajatasatru and Devadatta were both practicing the inverted [path]. First, [their action] kept evil persons from arising with the offense of inversion; second, they manifested the inverted conduct to gather in the class of evil. Hence the Mahamegha [Sutra] speaks of it as inconceivable, and the Lotus Sutra gives Devadatta the prophecy. If it were truly perpetrated, they would revolve without rest in the evil realms; how could they be companions of the Buddha life after life? (Direct Pointing commentary)
Ji 2: Asking about the place of rebirth.

"Only I beg the World-Honored One to speak widely for me of a place without sorrow and trouble; I wish to be reborn there, and take no delight in this defiled and evil world of Jambudvipa!" (Elaboration)

The passage has four sections: first, marking the gladness and loathing; second, describing what is to be loathed; third, establishing the vow of separation. Lingzhi says: these three sections set forth the essential technique of cultivation in the last age. If not for these, one would cultivate pure karma in vain and certainly not be reborn. Fourth, the direct request for the cause of rebirth.

This is the first, marking the gladness and loathing. "A place without sorrow and trouble": what Vaidehi asked, its wording is broad and inclusive; according to the Buddha's answer below, it points to the Pure Land. In the Saha world, with its five defilements, whether among men or among devas, there is sorrow and trouble. Only the Buddha's Pure Land, wherein both the subjective and objective rewards are supremely excellent, and only bliss is enjoyed, could it have sorrow? Jambudvipa is here translated "surpassing gold," specifically referring to the southern continent. According to the present context it generally refers to the great thousandfold Saha world, but it takes the near to make it easy to understand. Or perhaps among the four continents Jambudvipa's defilement and evil are the worst, so it is specially marked. (Lingzhi's Commentary)

"A place without sorrow and trouble" is to ask that the Pure Land Dharma be spoken. Only the Pure Land, where the highest good gather together, can be called without sorrow and without trouble. "I wish to be reborn there" is the vow of gladness for the Pure Land. "Taking no delight in Jambudvipa" is the mind of loathing. The two words, gladness and loathing, are what a cultivator of pure karma must never leave, and must not fail to know. (Elaboration)
"This defiled and evil place is filled with hells, hungry ghosts, and animals, and is a mass of much that is not good;"

Second, describing what is to be loathed. "Defiled" refers to the five defilements, namely wrong views, afflictions, and so on. All five are impure, so together they are called defiled. "Evil" refers to the ten evils, namely killing, stealing, and so on. The five defilements generally encompass both subjective and objective rewards, while the ten evils particularly point to the activities of the body and mind. If speaking of defilement and evil, in truth they cover all six realms; but the three evil paths of suffering are particularly raised to make the loathing clear. Throughout the great thousandfold world, hence it is said "filled." "A mass of much that is not good" is the gathering together of the evil destinies mentioned above in this place. Or it may point specifically to the small amount of good that remains among human beings, as below she wishes not to see evil persons. Whether kindred or enemy, obedient or rebellious, all are not good. Could Ajatasatru and Devadatta be a gathering of good? Above I followed the text in explanation. Now I will discuss by meaning: this defiled and evil place points to the dwellings of cities and villages in the world, where relatives and clans meet; among them the minds and actions differ in a thousand ways, and the three evil paths are filled, all being a mass of what is not good. Again, the defiled and evil place points to the present discriminating mind of we sentient beings; from beginningless time to the present, the boundless karmic seeds created by body, speech, and mind, and the three-evil-path activities daily arising, cannot be fully enumerated, hence it is said "filled" and "a mass of much that is not good." (Lingzhi's Commentary)
"May I, in a future life, not hear evil sounds, and not see evil persons."

Third, establishing the vow of separation. The five defilements and the three realms with their five rebellious acts and ten evils are all evil sounds; the sentient beings among them who commit such karma are all called evil persons. The Land of Ultimate Bliss has not even the name of evil destinies, so there are no evil sounds; the many superior good ones gather in one place, so there are no evil persons. (Lingzhi's Commentary)
"Now, to the World-Honored One I cast my five limbs to the ground, imploring compassion and repenting! Only I beg the Buddha's sun to teach me to contemplate the pure karma-ground!"

Fourth, the direct request for the cause of rebirth. Head and four limbs make the five parts of the body; the five places are all round, so they are also called the five wheels. Touching the ground is the weightiest of reverences. Because there was past offense, she suffers this affliction. Now wishing to be free of it, she must seek repentance. In Sanskrit "ksama" is here translated "repentance." Now speaking of the two, the Chinese and the Sanskrit are both used. Some say: repenting is to cut off the future, and regret is to be ashamed of the past. The Tathagata's teaching breaks through hindrances and removes doubt, like the sun illuminating the world, hence "the Buddha's sun." The subjective and objective rewards of the Land of Ultimate Bliss are all accomplished by the pure karma of the teacher and the assembly, so it is called the pure karma-ground. According to this, Vaidehi was directly seeking the method of contemplation, hence "teach me to contemplate." (Lingzhi's Commentary)

Now as to the Pure Land Dharma-gate: there are contemplation with images [visualization], contemplation of forms, holding the name, and contemplation of reality. Now that this lady begs to be taught to contemplate the pure karma-ground, the World-Honored One speaks for her the sixteen sublime contemplations. The four kinds above are all contained within them. The first twelve contemplations are contemplation with images; the thirteenth is contemplation of forms; the last three are holding the name. If one knows that the subjective contemplation and the objective contemplated are both inconceivable, that is contemplation of reality. (Elaboration)
Here ends the explanation of the introduction.

blocks.text: Jia 2: The main body, in three parts.

inline.s: First, emitting light and manifesting the lands to assess the capacities.
Second, the proper elucidation of the contemplations, the right cause of pure karma. Third, the assembly gains benefit.
Yi 1: Emitting light and manifesting the lands to assess the capacities, in three parts.
First, the Tathagata emits light and universally manifests the various lands.
Second, Vaidehi addresses the Buddha and selects a single direction. Third, Bimbisara, receiving the light, attains the fruit of the Way.
Bing 1: The Tathagata emits light and universally manifests the various lands.

At that time the World-Honored One emitted light from between his brows; that light, golden in color, universally illuminated the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions, then returned and dwelt on the Buddha's head, transforming into a golden platform like Mount Sumeru. The pure and wondrous lands of the Buddhas of the ten directions all appeared within it. Some lands were formed of the seven jewels; other lands were purely lotus flowers; other lands were like the palace of the lord of autonomous heaven; still other lands were like a crystal mirror. The lands of the ten directions all appeared within it, in such ways, immeasurable Buddha-lands, magnificently displayed and visible to see, so that Vaidehi might behold them.

The Tathagata has between his brows a white-hair mark, one zhang five [feet] long, five inches in circumference; on the outside it has eight ridges and is hollow within like a tube (the Contemplation of the Buddha's Samadhi Sutra says, "The hair-mark between the brows, one zhang and five [feet] long, emits light from within"), white as snow and shell; it curls to the right, signifying that from the middle path issues forth all dharmas (the Direct Pointing commentary says, "Between the brows signifies the middle way; the light signifies wisdom"). First scattered and then gathered, it also signifies gathering the many into the one. This reveals that this sutra is the pure, perfect, ultimate one-buddha-vehicle teaching, therefore this mark appears, different from ordinary times. The platform of light rises aloft, likened to Mount Sumeru. The lands manifest are immeasurable and cannot all be enumerated; briefly four are shown, to make them visible. Formed of seven jewels speaks of their dignity; purely lotus flowers speaks of their purity; like a heavenly palace speaks of their bliss; like a crystal mirror speaks of their bright clarity. As to the various lands, their splendor is extremely abundant; the sutra text, being concise, sets forth one characteristic for each, wishing to show that the Land of Ultimate Bliss possesses all these beauties together, and to let Vaidehi see them: this is the meaning of emitting light and manifesting the lands. (Lingzhi's Commentary)
Bing 2: Vaidehi addresses the Buddha and selects a single direction.

At that time Vaidehi said to the Buddha, "O World-Honored One! Though these Buddha-lands are pure and all have light, I now wish to be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, at the place of Amitabha Buddha. Only I beg the World-Honored One to teach me contemplation and teach me right concentration."

According to Vaidehi's words: the lands of the ten directions are all pure in appearance, with nowhere not good; as to my seeking rebirth, I will be born in only one place. Having received the World-Honored One's compassionate manifestation so as to contemplate, it is only to make me choose for myself. I now wish to be born in Amitabha Buddha's land. This sufficiently proves that that Buddha's bond of connection with sentient beings of this world is deep. (Elaboration)

The World-Honored One emitted light between his brows and manifested the pure lands, letting Vaidehi choose for herself: because among the Buddha-lands, pure and luminous, none surpasses the Land of Ultimate Bliss; seeing it with her own fleshly eyes, her faith and joy would be doubly deep. From this contemplation she at once obtained right concentration. (Brief Treatise)
The passage has three sections: first, a general statement that the various lands are not what she wishes.

Second, from "I now" onward, she particularly points to the Land of Ultimate Bliss as exactly matching her capacity. The reason is that sentient beings of this inferior world have minds much scattered; if one does not point to a single direction and contemplate a single Buddha fixedly, the contemplation is hard to accomplish and rebirth is much obstructed. Besides, Amitabha's light always shines and his vow is vast and deep. Therefore, being born in one land, one is connected to all lands; contemplating one Buddha, one sees all Buddhas alike. The Treatise on Ten Doubts says the Buddha answered Pukwang [spoke:] the principle is clearly evident. Shandao's exclusive practice accords with the same meaning. Third, from "only I beg" onward, she requests the contemplative method for the practice of rebirth. The first stage of practice, directing the mind toward the contemplated object, is called contemplation. When the contemplation is accomplished and harmoniously still from the wheel of itself, it is called right concentration. As the earth-contemplation says, "To have such a thought is called a coarse vision of the earth of the Land of Ultimate Bliss," which is contemplation; "if one attains samadhi, one sees that land's earth clearly and distinctly, beyond all description," which is right concentration. One may know that contemplation and right concentration both belong to the contemplative method, differing only in depth. And earlier it said: "teach me to contemplate the pure karma-ground," showing that Vaidehi only asked for contemplation. (Lingzhi's Commentary)

The Direct Pointing commentary says: measuring with a scattered mind is called contemplation, spoken with reference to wisdom; fixing the mind single-mindedly is called right concentration, spoken with reference to concentration.

The Annotated Notes say: after the mind is settled there is no thought and no thinking; but the single-minded thought before settling is called contemplation. The Four-fascicle Commentary says: contemplation is the expedient prior to concentration. Right concentration, also called samadhi, is another name for meditative absorption. Free from the wrong and scattered is called right; receiving the Dharma into the mind without thought and without thinking is called concentration, like a bright mirror reflecting objects with no mind of its own. The Profound Meaning of the Contemplation Sutra says: as to right concentration, thinking mind is entirely still, and deliberating and reflecting both vanish, corresponding to samadhi; this is called right concentration. (Annotated Notes)
Bing 3: Bimbisara, receiving the light, attains the fruit of the Way.

At that time the World-Honored One straightway smiled, and a five-colored light issued from the Buddha's mouth; each light shone on the crown of King Bimbisara's head. At that time the great king, though confined, was unimpeded in the eye of his mind; from afar he saw the World-Honored One and bowed his head in reverence; and by himself he advanced, attaining the fruit of an Anagamin.

The Tathagata's manifestation of the lands was precisely for this purpose; the capacity and the stimulus met, hiddenly communicated and secretly responding, so the Buddha smiled. The Contemplation of the Buddha's Ocean of Marks Sutra says, "It is the constant law of the Buddhas that whenever they smile, a five-colored light always issues from the mouth." The light shone on the king's crown — the Buddha's power of blessing caused him to increase in the fruit of the Way. Receiving the light and seeing the Buddha, he deeply realized impermanence, raised wisdom, and cut off delusions, and so realized the third fruit. Anagamin is here rendered "no return." His remaining fetters were nearly exhausted, and he would not return to the lower worlds. According to this, Bimbisara, seeing the Buddha and attaining the fruit, should have heard the contemplative teaching together with the lady; but later, in concluding the benefit, it says the Buddha only taught Vaidehi and five hundred maids, from which we know that Bimbisara, having realized the fruit, already passed away. (Lingzhi's Commentary)

The smile has two intentions: first, answering the lady's cause of joy, hence the happy smile; second, completing the great king's fruit of joy, hence the happy smile. (The Annotated Notes say, "The Buddha does not smile idly; only when fulfilling the fundamental purpose of his appearance in the world does he begin to smile in assent. Thus the Buddha's smile manifests his fundamental purpose in appearing in the world.") That without waiting for her reply, the light first shone upon the king: first, to let them see the Buddha and the assembly so as to cut off doubt and dissolve fetters; second, to let them realize that worldly dharmas are all like dreams and illusions; third, to let them believe that good and evil and their fruits are never mistaken; fourth, to let them know that each gains the benefit of his own cultivation and realization. The five colors signify breaking the five aggregates and becoming the joy of the five-part Dharma-body, and surpassing the five defilements to attain the five purities. (Direct Pointing commentary)

The commentary says: "That he did not directly answer the cause of her land, but again emitted light and smiled, has two intentions: first, it was to (cause the king to) progress in the Way; second, it was to let the king and the lady see one another. The king, having seen the light and progressed in the Way, knew the country was not real, and looked on death as on sleep; the lady, seeing the king without sorrow, had the fruit of the contemplative method accomplished. The smile is like when the Sakya clan was slain, the Tathagata's light and color became all the more manifest. It is precisely because the Tathagata well understands that karma and its retribution are unfailing, and that when the time comes one cannot flee. The king, though destined to die, obtained the trace of the Way; the lady's imprisonment is the very moment of manifesting the Pure Land. Having so many conditions, therefore he smiled." I privately reflect: since Bimbisara's fruit had ripened and fallen, the time had come and the principle was evident; so he first emitted light to touch him, enabling him to leave the cage and become a sage-fruit. Besides, that lesser vessel of his naturally accomplished a lesser fruit; it was not only that Vaidehi was the initiator of this sutra and also the one of the assembly, while Bimbisara had neither of these matters, hence he was made to be released first. Had Bimbisara not [been born during] Ajatasatru's [reign], he would not necessarily have attained a sage-fruit in this present life. Even if he attained it in this life, it would not necessarily be so swift. Had Ajatasatru not met an evil friend, he would not necessarily have had the thought of killing his father and seizing the kingdom; without this utmost evil mind, he would by no means commit this inverted deed. That the world's most extreme evil cause of suffering should help accomplish the good fruit of sagehood beyond the world — is this not inconceivable! Bimbisara, because his own son killed his father and sought the kingdom, from this [suffering] his worldly thoughts became like cold ashes; and when he was shut in the seven-layered chamber, not hearing the least of state affairs, at this time he returned to his original face, and together with upholding the precepts and hearing the Dharma, cultivated the three studies together — therefore he cut off delusion and realized truth; that is fitting! That the light was five-colored signifies that from the Buddha's Dharma-nature, upon the substance of the five aggregates, a wonderful light was revealed, which broke through Bimbisara's five aggregates and transformed them into the fruit of the five-part Dharma-body. Therefore though the king was confined, his body and mind within and without were all at ease. The seven-layered walls of the chamber could in no way obstruct; though it is said he saw from afar, it was as if before his eyes. At the instant of bowing, he realized the third fruit. In Sanskrit, Anagamin, in Chinese, "no return," meaning he had already cut off the nine grades of birth-causes of the desire realm, so he could no longer come to the lower worlds to take birth. (Elaboration)
The Annotated Notes say: the mind that contemplates, through its power of insight, illuminates and knows all dharmas — this is called the eye of the mind.
The Jingying commentary says: the king was first a Stream-enterer, so now he advanced and became an Anagamin.
Yi 2: The proper elucidation of the contemplations, the right cause of pure karma, in two parts.

blocks.text: First, the general statement and the promise to speak. Second, the particular exposition of the pure contemplations.

inline.s: Bing 1: The general statement and the promise to speak, in two parts.
First, the general statement.
Second, the promise to speak.
Ding 1: The general statement.
At that time the World-Honored One told Vaidehi: "Do you now know? Amitabha Buddha is not far from here. You should fix your thought and contemplate closely that land accomplished by pure karma.

First asking whether she knows is to make clear that the Pure Land is not something the Buddha speaks of by himself, with no one else knowing [the capacity]. The Amitabha Sutra says, "To the west from here, passing over a hundred thousand Buddha-lands," yet it says it is not far; there are three explanations: first, from the Buddha-eye's contemplation, as the Surangama Sutra says: the celestial eye contemplates the great thousandfold, even as looking at a fruit in the palm; how much more the Buddha-eye! For example, ascending on high and looking down, one eye takes in ten thousand leagues; this is what is meant by "ascending Mount Tai and the whole world becomes small." Second, from the swiftness of thought: the spirit-mind is unimpeded, and distant regions and foreign lands, at the very rise of a thought, are reached; this is what is meant by "thought is swifter than the wind." Third, from the Buddha's power of gathering in: though one has not attained transcendent power, riding the Buddha's spiritual power, as the Treatise on Ten Doubts says, an inferior man, mounted with a world-turning king, in one day and night traverses the four continents; this is what is meant by "a blue fly attached to a steed's tail." (Lingzhi's Commentary)

The Miaozong Sub-commentary says: "Speaking of 'not far' is because by the Buddha's power, one who cultivates contemplation sees it the moment he wishes. Therefore this passage says, 'you should fix your thought and contemplate closely that land.' Hence we know that the Buddha's power enables one who wishes to see, so that when the contemplation is accomplished he sees. Later it says, 'All sentient beings who contemplate the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, by the Buddha's power, shall see that pure land.' Therefore the Pratyutpanna [samadhi] seeing the Buddha discusses three powers: first, the Buddha's power; second, samadhi power; third, the practitioner's own fundamental merit-power."
The Annotated Notes say: "Fixing thought means to fix the thought on one place and not think of another. 'Closely' means to examine carefully."

The Jingying commentary says: "'Contemplate closely that land' encourages contemplation of the objective reward; 'accomplished by pure karma' encourages contemplation of the subjective reward." That is, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas and the persons of the three grades of rebirth and so on are called those accomplished by pure karma. The Lingzhi commentary says: "Those accomplished by pure karma is a general term for the subjective and objective rewards of that land." The Direct Pointing commentary says: "Those accomplished by pure karma in that land: the immeasurable splendor of the Land of Ultimate Bliss is all the perfuming and accomplishment of taintless virtue of nature, and the accomplishment of the pure karma of blessing."

The Elaboration says: "The Buddha's meaning is this: earlier you said you wished to be born in Amitabha's Land of Ultimate Bliss; now he tells Vaidehi: 'Do you now know? Amitabha Buddha's Land of Ultimate Bliss is not far from here and not hard to be reborn in; just fix your thought on Amitabha Buddha and contemplate closely that Land of Ultimate Bliss.'"
Ding 2: The promise to speak.
"I now will speak for you widely of many similes; and also cause all ordinary people of future ages who wish to cultivate pure karma to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss."

"I now will speak for you widely of many similes" is the promise to speak. From "and also cause" onward sets forth the intention of speaking. That he speaks is to benefit sentient beings of the present and future. (Jiaxiang's Commentary)

The realm of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, sentient beings have not yet known; taking things as comparisons, hence "many similes." As below, "like a thousand million suns," "its light like flowers," and so on. Or perhaps all the words of explanation are generally called similes. "And also cause future [beings]" precisely reveals the fundamental intention, not limited to those of the present assembly. This is what is meant by a bow of a thousand catties; would it be triggered merely for a field-mouse? (Lingzhi's Commentary)

blocks.text: Bing 2: The particular exposition of the pure contemplations, in two parts.

inline.s: First, setting forth the three kinds of meritorious karma; second, explaining the sixteen contemplations.
Ding 1: Setting forth the three kinds of meritorious karma, in three parts.
First, the general heading.
Second, the particular explanation. Third, the concluding praise.

The reason for first making clear the three blessings: they are the appropriate undertakings of one who cultivates contemplation. Without contemplation there is nothing to guide his merit; without merit there is nothing to accomplish his contemplation. With contemplation and no merit, one lacks the adornments; with merit and no contemplation, one is drawn toward other destinies. Lacking adornments, the reward obtained is not supreme; drawn toward other destinies, there is no way to rebirth. The two methods support each other, and there is no place where they do not benefit. In addressing those who study, apply the mind with determination to investigate; do not be confused at the crossroads and lose the starting point of your own advance. (Lingzhi's Commentary)

The Brief Treatise says: "About to explain the pure contemplations, he first teaches beings to cultivate the three blessings: because by worldly dharmas one gradually reaches supramundane dharmas. It is like storing nectar: first clean the vessel; if the vessel is not clean, its flavor is spoiled."
Wu 1: The general heading.
"Those who wish to be born in that land should cultivate the three blessings:"
The Lingzhi commentary says: "'Those who wish to be born' speaks of their aspiration; 'should cultivate' instructs that they must do so."
Wu 2: The particular explanation.
"First, to honor and care for one's parents, to serve one's teachers and elders, to be of compassionate mind and not kill, and to cultivate the ten wholesome deeds."

Since these are the cause of the Buddhas of the three times, one knows clearly they are the great practice of the Bodhisattva. The first is the karma shared with ordinary people; the second is the karma shared with the two vehicles; the third is the Mahayana karma not shared [with them]. (The Direct Pointing commentary says, "the third shares the Mahayana karma.") Within the first, the upper two clauses are the practice of repaying kindness. Parents have the kindness of giving birth and nurture; teachers and elders have the kindness of instruction. The lower two clauses are the practice of abandoning evil. Not killing is the foremost of the ten wholesome deeds, so it is particularly marked. The body avoids the three wrong-doings, the mouth leaves the four faults, and the mind cuts off the three evils. (Lingzhi's Commentary)

Honoring and caring for one's parents: sentient beings, depending on parents, have this body; depending on this body, they come to know there is a Buddha. Therefore, not revering one's own body, one does not accomplish the wisdom of all seeds; not revering one's own parents, one cannot grow all the fields of merit. Some may say: the Tathagata left his family and went forth, which seems to contradict the principle of filial care. They do not know that there is the filiality of the world and the filiality of the world-transcending. The filiality of the world: while they live, provide for them fully; when they die, sacrifice to them fully; establish one's person in the Way and make one's name known to later generations — that is all. The filiality of the world-transcending must await one's parents' escape from the three realms and realization of the unconditioned; only then is the way of the son fulfilled. Great filiality honors one's parents; what exceeds this? (Brief Treatise)

Serving one's teachers and elders: there are worldly teachers and elders and world-transcending teachers and elders. Leading one in the arts of poetry and books, urging one along the path of benevolence and duty — these are worldly teachers and elders. Awakening one by the teachings of the three jewels, advancing one by the gate of the two truths — these are world-transcending teachers and elders. That they ought to be served is one and the same. (Brief Treatise)

Of compassionate mind and not killing: the Buddha's mind is great compassion. Among the evil karmas of the Saha world, none exceeds killing life; the enmities and hatreds of age after age arise from killing. If the mind of killing is not cut off, the mind of compassion is not fulfilled; if the mind of compassion is not fulfilled, one stands opposed and separate from sentient beings; standing opposed and separate from sentient beings is to stand opposed and separate from the Tathagata. To wish to seek rebirth in the Pure Land is difficult! (Brief Treatise)
"Second, to receive and uphold the three refuges, to be complete in the various precepts, and not to transgress the rules of deportment."

The upper clause is the three refuges that turn from the false. Ordinary people from beginningless time are bound to the devil; performing the rite and taking refuge, they seek deliverance and protection. If one only takes refuge, there is good but no precepts. If one receives the many precepts, one must also take the three refuges. The lower two clauses are the reception of the precept dharmas. For householders, the five and eight; for renunciates, the ten and the complete precepts; hence "the various precepts." Receiving and upholding without deficiency, hence "complete." Deportment is also precept, subtle and light, hard to hold, which people commonly trespass, so it is particularly marked and singled out. (Lingzhi's Commentary)

If one can cultivate the ten wholesome deeds and counter the ten evil deeds, then past hindrances gradually dissolve; past hindrances dissolved, hence rebirth is unimpeded. Yet one must receive them with the three refuges and widen them with the many precepts: without receiving the three refuges, one cannot plant the seed of the world-transcending; without being complete in the many precepts, one cannot cultivate the foundation of the world-transcending. The three refuges and the many precepts are the right cause of entering Buddhahood. (Brief Treatise)
"Third, to rouse the bodhi-mind, to believe deeply in cause and effect, to read and recite the Mahayana, and to encourage those who practice."

Within it are four clauses: the first is to rouse the great mind. Bodhi is translated "the Way," that is, the mind of the supreme Way. The second is to arouse great faith. Good and evil and their cause and effect all come from one's own mind; knowing this with awe and caution, hence "believe deeply." The third is to produce great understanding. The teaching conveys the original wisdom, which is produced by recitation. The fourth is to cultivate the great practice. To encourage and entice toward cultivation, not causing one to fall back. The first three are self-practice; the last one is the conversion of others. (Lingzhi's Commentary)

Yet although one is complete in refuge and precepts, if one does not rouse the bodhi-mind, though one had merit and fortune, in the end it becomes tainted and out-flowing; because it does not correspond to the Tathagata's seal of wisdom that relies on nothing. (Brief Treatise)

Bodhi is anciently translated "the Way," newly translated "awakening." The Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom, chapter forty-one: "When a Bodhisattva first rouses the mind, anchoring on the supreme Way, thinking 'I shall become a Buddha' — this is called the bodhi-mind." The Jingying commentary: "Bodhi is the Way. The Buddha-fruit is completely perfect and penetrating, called bodhi. To raise the intention and direct toward it is called rousing the mind. To speak of it in brief: what the Buddha attained, I also shall attain." The Four-fascicle Commentary: "Bodhi is the name of the Buddha-fruit; mind is the seeking-mind of sentient beings. Hence the phrase 'to rouse the bodhi-mind.'"

Believing deeply in cause and effect: doing good obtains fortune, doing evil obtains calamity; like ginseng, which is foremost in tonifying, and rhubarb, which is foremost in purging. Toning and purging lie in the person, completely from one's fundamental endowment. Hence we know that doing good is itself fortune, and outside good there is no fortune; doing evil is itself calamity, and outside evil there is no calamity. This is called cause and effect being simultaneous. Then, in a single thought of mindfulness of the Buddha, that thought is the Buddha; thought after thought of mindfulness, there is no thought that is not Buddha. The mind being pure and the Land being pure is likewise. (Brief Treatise)

Reading and reciting the Mahayana: if one does not read the Mahayana, one does not understand the Buddha's mind; not understanding the Buddha's mind, one does not accord with the Buddha's wisdom; not according with the Buddha's wisdom, though he be born in that land, he cannot see the Buddha. If one in truth understands the Buddha's mind, and in truth accords with the Buddha's wisdom, benefiting self and benefiting others, the capacity cannot be restrained, because the Buddha and sentient beings are of one substance. (Brief Treatise)
Wu 3: The concluding praise, in two parts.
First, the conclusive statement.
Second, the praise of its excellence.
Ji 1: The conclusive statement.
"Such these three matters are called pure karma."
Ji 2: The praise of its excellence.
The Buddha told Vaidehi: "Do you now know? These three kinds of karma are the pure karma right cause of the Buddhas of the three times — past, future, and present."
The meritorious fruit of the three times is accomplished by means of this, hence it is called the right cause. (Lingzhi's Commentary)

The Brief Treatise says: "When the three blessings are cultivated together, the pure cause is complete; whether one contemplates or recites, it follows whatever one seeks. It is like holding a mirror to take an image, or raising a voice to require an echo — how far off is it?"
